title: A Border for the Asset
premise: Jonah Villalobos, a disgraced intelligence analyst working deniable cases for whoever pays, is hired to trace a voiceprint that unlocks a black server in Malta. The voice belongs to Mara Reyes, a whistleblower he once burned to save his own career, and the server holds proof of a transnational trafficking network protected by the very agencies that discarded him. As hunters close in, Jonah assembles an unlikely crew—a retired border agent, a teenage hacker, and Mara herself—who become the family he never had. In the end, Jonah chooses exposure over survival, trading his last valuable secret (his own buried identity) to detonate the network publicly, finding justice outside the law and belonging at the cost of the invisibility that once defined him.
about_author: E. M. Dunmore is the pen name of a former policy researcher who spent a decade writing about migration and institutional failure before turning to fiction. They live near a land border they cross often, and write about people who cannot.

chapters.title: The Quiet Client
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Working from a rented room in Nogales, Jonah takes a no-attribution job tracing a voiceprint fragment for a client who pays in untraceable crypto. He rationalizes the work as harmless pattern-matching, but a detail in the audio—an old radio jingle—snags something personal. Beat: loneliness disguised as professionalism.

chapters.title: Voiceprint
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The voiceprint matches Mara Reyes, the analyst whose testimony Jonah suppressed years ago to keep his clearance. She's alive, and she's been feeding data into a locked server in Malta. He should walk away; instead he runs her name through dead archives. Beat: guilt resurfacing like a body in water.

chapters.title: Three Agencies, No Home
chapters.summary: Flashback-heavy chapter, Jonah's POV. We learn how Jonah was bounced from three agencies, each exit tied to doing the right thing too late or too quietly. Present-day: his handler warns him the client's request has tripped internal flags. Beat: the cost of being the man nobody claims.

chapters.title: The Border Agent
chapters.summary: Rosa Ibarra's POV. Rosa, a retired border patrol agent turned fixer, is hired separately to find 'the man with the voice problem.' She recognizes the job's shape—it's a cleanup, not an investigation—and starts keeping her own file. Beat: conscience over contract.

chapters.title: Malta Opens
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Using Mara's voiceprint against a biometric gate, Jonah cracks the server and finds shipping manifests linking a humanitarian corridor to a trafficking pipeline—with agency fingerprints all over it. Someone pings the server while he's inside. Beat: awe curdling into fear.

chapters.title: They Know Your Name
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. His safehouse is compromised; he runs with two drives and nothing else. A contact confirms the client was never a client—it was bait to see who'd come looking. Beat: paranoia becoming clarity—he was never invisible, just unwatched until now.

chapters.title: Sixteen and Faster Than You
chapters.summary: Teo's POV. Teo, a sixteen-year-old hacker squatting in an abandoned customs office, intercepts Jonah's panicked traffic and offers help—for a price: teach me how you did it. Jonah, against every instinct, says yes. Beat: first crack in the armor; found family begins.

chapters.title: What Mara Buried
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. In hiding in Lisbon, Mara reveals she built the Malta server as insurance after surviving an attempt on her life. She's been waiting years for someone with the skills—and the shame—to open it. Beat: guarded hope meeting earned distrust.

chapters.title: Rosa's File
chapters.summary: Rosa's POV. Rosa confronts Jonah instead of delivering him, laying out what she knows: three prior assets who opened that server all died within a month. She joins them—not for justice, she says, but because she's tired of watching borders protect the wrong people. Beat: alliance forged from shared disillusionment.

chapters.title: The Corridor
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The team traces the trafficking route through the manifests: people moved under cover of legitimate aid convoys, logged and erased by cooperating officials. Teo finds a live feed still running. Beat: horror at scale; the case stops being abstract.

chapters.title: A Name Worth Killing For
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Decoding the deepest layer, Jonah finds the linchpin: a serving director whose signature authorizes the corridor. Also in the files: Jonah's own old suppression memo, annotated in Mara's hand. Beat: the secret worth killing for turns out to be his own complicity.

chapters.title: Teo Gets Careless
chapters.summary: Teo's POV. Teo brags online to impress an old forum friend and leads a hunter straight to the customs office. Jonah arrives mid-breach, gets them both out, but the team's location is burned. Beat: found family means someone can now be taken from you.

chapters.title: Lisbon, Briefly
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The four converge in Lisbon. Mara and Jonah finally speak plainly about what he did to her testimony; she doesn't forgive him, but she stops needing him punished. Beat: reckoning without absolution—the honest kind of repair.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Through back channels, the director's people offer Jonah full reinstatement, cleared record, protection—if he hands over the drives and Mara. They know exactly what a man with no agency wants. Beat: temptation aimed precisely at the wound.

chapters.title: Counterweight
chapters.summary: Rosa's POV. Rosa lays out their real options: run, sell, or go public through journalists she trusts from her border years. Running protects them; going public probably kills some of them. She asks each to choose out loud. Beat: the team becomes a family by choosing each other over safety.

chapters.title: Dead Drop Protocol
chapters.summary: Teo's POV. Teo builds a dead-man's-switch release: if any of them are taken, everything publishes automatically. While testing it, he discovers the hunters have a mole inside the journalist's outlet. Beat: competence and dread in equal measure; the plan has a heartbeat now.

chapters.title: The Trap That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah lets himself be 'captured' to feed false drive locations through the mole, buying time—but the interrogation reveals the director plans to move the corridor's next convoy in seventy-two hours, with real people aboard. Beat: the con works, and it doesn't matter; the clock outruns the trick.

chapters.title: Seventy-Two Hours
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs, intercut. The team splits: Rosa and Mara intercept the convoy documentation chain; Teo and Jonah race to verify the final ledger copy before the servers are wiped. Every thread frays at once. Beat: rising action at full sprint; sacrifice becomes inevitable.

chapters.title: What Jonah Trades
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Cornered at the Malta node, Jonah makes the trade promised by the blurb: he surrenders his last secret—his real identity, buried since his second firing—as authentication to pull the master ledger before the wipe completes. The hunters get a name; the world gets the files. Beat: climax; identity spent like currency, willingly.

chapters.title: Convoy 9
chapters.summary: Rosa's POV. Rosa physically blocks the corridor checkpoint long enough for Mara's evidence packet to reach three outlets simultaneously, forcing officials to halt the convoy rather than perform for cameras. She takes a beating; she doesn't take a bullet. Beat: justice outside the law, paid for in blood and nerve.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Unattributed
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The publications detonate; the director falls; investigations bloom. Jonah is officially a ghost again—no credit, no record—but this time by choice, with the dead-man's-switch holding the rest in reserve. Mara publishes under her own name. Beat: resolution; visibility chosen, not imposed.

chapters.title: A Border for the Asset
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, epilogue. Months later, the four share a cramped kitchen near the border Rosa once patrolled—no agency, no client, a new case on the table that no one else will touch. Jonah realizes the border he needed wasn't around himself but between him and the people who used him. Beat: belonging, quiet and hard-won; the family holds.
